title: Design a Distributed Key-Value Store
oneLiner: Dynamo or Cassandra as a 45-minute design round: consistent hashing, quorums, conflict resolution, repair and LSM storage.
keyTakeaway: A Dynamo-style store spreads keys over a ring with virtual nodes, keeps N copies in different zones, and lets each request choose its consistency with R and W quorums. Choosing availability means replicas will diverge, so the design needs ways to resolve conflicts (last-write-wins or vector clocks) and to repair replicas (hinted handoff, read repair, Merkle-tree anti-entropy), on top of a write-optimised LSM storage engine.
explanation:
Same format as the other walk-throughs: write your answer for each stage first, then compare it with the model answer and tick what you covered.

This one is different from the product designs. There's no feed or redirect to optimise; you are building the database the other designs used. The API is three operations, so almost all the time goes on how the data is placed, copied and kept correct. The decision that shapes everything comes in the requirements stage: when some replicas are unreachable, does the store reject the write or accept it and reconcile later? Dynamo chose to accept it, and every later stage follows from that: sloppy quorums, conflicting versions, and background repair. Say the choice out loud and connect it to CAP and PACELC.

In the estimation stage, notice that disk space, not request rate, sets the node count, and that rebuilding a failed node is a number worth computing because it's the argument for virtual nodes. The deep dive is a menu of techniques (consistent hashing, R + W > N, last-write-wins versus vector clocks, hinted handoff, Merkle trees, gossip with phi accrual failure detection, LSM trees and compaction), and you won't cover all of them in 15 minutes. Interviewers usually pick two or three; explain the mechanism and what it costs, for example that last-write-wins silently drops one of two concurrent writes, or that skipping repair for longer than the tombstone grace period brings deleted data back. Expect follow-ups such as "a whole zone just went down: which reads and writes still succeed?"
